chapters.label: A fake app in the group

scenes.visual: Cards: Shared in a group; Free and offline; Stole saved passwords.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A fake AI app went round our school group. It was called “SuperTutor AI free”, and it promised a better chatbot, offline. It stole the passwords saved on three phones.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Check before you trust a model
scenes.narration: Today: how AI models and apps reach you, and how to check one before you trust it.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Training data; Model file; Code and app; Your phone.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Every AI tool is built from parts made by others: training data, a model file, code and an app. That chain of parts is the supply chain. Any link can be faked, or changed on the way to you.

scenes.visual: A list: A fake copy; Changed on the way; Runs code when loaded.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Three things go wrong. A fake copy pretends to be the real model. A real file is changed on the way, by one byte or a million. And some model files can run hidden code the moment you load them.

scenes.visual: One big value, 64: hex characters, from any file.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The first check is a fingerprint. SHA-256 turns any file into sixty-four hex characters. Change one byte, and about half of them change. If yours matches the one the real publisher posted, the bytes are the same.

scenes.visual:
Code typed out on a card:
import hashlib, binascii
h = hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
fp = binascii.hexlify(h).decode()
print(fp == published)
scenes.animation: The code types itself out; the highlighted line lights up.
scenes.narration: In Python it takes three lines. Hash the file's bytes, turn the result into hex, and compare it with the published fingerprint. Equal means unchanged.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You change one letter inside a model file. What happens to its fingerprint?

scenes.visual: Two columns. Fingerprint: Proves: same bytes. Signature: Proves: who made it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: About half changes, so even a tiny edit can't hide. But a fingerprint only proves the bytes didn't change. It can't tell you who made them. For that, you need a signature.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The publisher signs the file with a secret key, and anyone can check it with their public key. An impostor can post a fake with its own fingerprint, but they can't sign as the real publisher.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Official source only; Check fingerprint and signature; Keep a list of your models.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So build three habits. Download only from the official source. Check the fingerprint and the signature before you run anything. And keep a list of the models you use: name, version, where from, fingerprint.

scenes.visual: A list: Genuine: both green; One byte changed: half flips; Impostor: signature fails.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: is this the real model?
scenes.narration: In the app, leave the file genuine: both checks are green. Change one byte: about half the fingerprint flips. Then try the impostor: the bytes look fine, but the signature fails.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A model's fingerprint matches the one posted right next to it, on a site you don't know. Can you trust it?

scenes.visual: The summary: Any link can be faked; Fingerprint: the same bytes; Signature: who made it; Official source, both checks, a list. Takeaway: Before you run a model, check where it came from.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Faked links · Fingerprint · Signature · A list
scenes.narration: Not yet: whoever posted the file posted that fingerprint too. Remember: any link in the chain can be faked. A fingerprint proves the same bytes, and a signature proves who made them. Use official sources, check both, and keep a list.

scenes.visual: A list: AI apps on a family phone; Where did each come from?; Remove what you can't check; Start your model list.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: with the owner, look at the AI apps on a family phone. Write where each came from: the store, a shared file or a website. Remove what you can't check, and start your model list.

checkpoints.prompt: You change one letter inside a model file. What happens to its SHA-256 fingerprint?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: about half flips, so even a tiny edit can't hide.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: one changed byte flips about half the fingerprint. That's why it catches any edit.
